data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories unavoidably smuggles in induction because any rational basis for preferring one unrefuted theory over another for future action implicitly assumes the uniformity of nature or the reliability of past survival as a guide to future performance.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If Popper can demonstrate a form of rationality that does not rely on expectations of future regularity.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'preference' can be shown to be purely aesthetic or conventional, lacking any predictive component.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'uniformity' assumed is a tautology of the testing framework rather than a claim about the world.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism is a pragmatic analysis of 'action.' To act on Theory A rather than Theory B is to expect A to yield better results. If this expectation is not based on the probability of A being true (which Popper denies), it must be based on the assumption that the conditions which allowed A to survive will persist. This assumption is the Principle of Uniformity, which is inductive. Therefore, Popper's 'critical preference' is merely induction by another name, disguised as a methodological rule.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
